slides.title: Keep connector C: redesign it now, fix bundle service, and decide any 2029 sunset on evidence

paragraphs.text: Keep connector C: redesign it now, fix bundle service, and decide any 2029 sunset on evidence
Board question: should Vesper discontinue low reported-margin sterile connector C and redeploy the team to connector D? Pre-read for the February 2027 board meeting
Vesper MedTech
Board of Directors
Synthetic benchmark data · US$ millions, FY2026 full year, from the board briefing pack

slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Do not discontinue C in 2027: exiting destroys cash and breaches board constraints. Redesign C, fix bundle service and make any sunset a 2029 decision
C's 8% margin comes from the cost allocation; on contribution margin, C is actually the portfolio's strongest connector
–	C earns $3.8M of direct contribution, a 63% margin, compared with 50% for D and A and 42% for B
–	Only $0.4M of C's $3.3M allocated cost is avoidable; the other $2.9M would move onto A, B and D
Exiting C in 2027 loses $4.75M in the first year and $2.65M every year after, and breaks two non-negotiables
–	Even at the optimistic 25% migration D adds only $0.75M; break-even needs $6.8M of D sales (113% of C)
–	The $2.1M penalty alone is 2.3 times the $0.9M envelope; C is in 9 of 14 major bundles, with no validated substitute
The customer case for exit does not hold up: the real problem is bundle fill, caused by A and B
–	The 9-percentage-point renewal gap is confounded by size, equipment and coverage, with no before/after test
–	C's 98% on-time figure omits A/B bundle misses; bundle fill is 91% against 95%, and exit would not fix it
Recommended: redesign C now (+$2.4M over 2027–29), recover bundle fill, then hand the team to D
–	The $0.55M redesign pays back in about 5 months, breaks even at 19% of the saving and fits the $0.9M
–	Renew the two bundles without exit notice, with a consent-based D path; Q4 2028 gate on any 2029 sunset

Our starting hypothesis, "keep C", survived four of five tests; the fifth showed that keeping C unchanged is not enough
Initial hypothesis, set before testing: retain C, because its low reported margin is an allocation effect rather than an avoidable economic cost

data: 1. C earns more cash than its exit would save
$3.8M direct contribution against $0.4M avoidable fixed cost: exit gives up a net $3.4M a year before migration
2. D cannot replace what C earns
Ceiling of 25% of C revenue = $1.5M (all of D's spare capacity) × 50% = $0.75M, against $3.4M at stake
$2.1M first-year penalties against $0.9M approved cash; C in 9 of 14 major bundles; no substitute validated on every hospital model
4. C is not driving customer attrition
9-percentage-point renewal gap is correlational and confounded (size, legacy equipment, coverage); no before/after evidence
Bundle fill 91% against 95% required; C faces price pressure; a $1.25M a year redesign saving costs $0.55M

Fails: refine
Revised answer: keep C, but not unchanged. Fund the redesign, restore 95% bundle fill, use the renewals to open a consent-based path to D, and decide any 2029 sunset in Q4 2028 on observed evidence

paragraphs.text: 1 Profitability    2 Exit cost    3 Customers    4 Plan
The renewal gap does not show C causes churn: size, legacy equipment and coverage confound it, and it is untested
The claim: accounts that buy C renew less often, so C causes it
Three factors the comparison does not control for
Tests to run before the Q4 2028 gate
▪	The CEO reads a scatter of hospital renewal rates by product mix as C causing dissatisfaction
▪	Correlation, not causation: C accounts differ systematically from the rest
▪	No counterfactual: no before/after evidence that removing C raises retention
▪	It cannot support exit, and it cannot rule out a C effect either
▪	Smaller hospitals on legacy equipment (named in the briefing pack)
▪	Lower customer-success coverage (named in the briefing pack)
▪	Bundle fill of 91% at the nine C-bundle customers, caused by A/B misses: a further plausible confounder (our hypothesis, untested; the pack does not link it to renewals)
▪	Each of these could lower renewal on its own
▪	Compare renewal within matched segments (size × equipment age × customer-success coverage)
▪	Control for the bundle fill each account actually received
▪	Code lost-account exit reasons for any mention of C
▪	Track retention of any accounts that drop C or move to D
▪	Only a gap that persists within segments feeds the sunset decision, valued against the $3.4M a year C contributes
